Stellar properties: mass, luminosity, temperature, and color, with color-temperature ordering (hotter bluer, cooler redder) and mass as the key driver (mass-luminosity relation)

Spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, M as a temperature-ordering device (with Cannon's mnemonic)
Apparent versus absolute magnitude, named simply with a standard reference distance
Binary stars briefly, as the way stellar masses are measured

The inverse-square falloff of apparent brightness with distance

Roughly half of stars are binaries; first binary discovered in 1650

claims.claim: Stars are giant balls of hot gas, mostly hydrogen, with some helium and small amounts of other elements, that make their own light.

A star shines because nuclear fusion in its core fuses hydrogen into helium; the released energy heats the star and prevents it from collapsing under gravity, so a star is a balance between inward gravity and outward fusion pressure.
Stars that are stably fusing hydrogen into helium are called main-sequence stars, and the Milky Way contains more than 100 billion stars.

Luminosity is the total amount of energy a star emits per second at all wavelengths; apparent brightness is what we measure from Earth and depends on both luminosity and distance, falling with the square of the distance.

The color of a star indicates its surface temperature: blue-white stars are much hotter than the Sun and red stars are cooler; OpenStax Table 17.1 examples run blue about 25,000 K (Spica), white about 10,000 K (Vega), yellow about 6,000 K (Sun), orange about 4,000 K (Aldebaran), red about 3,000 K (Betelgeuse).

More massive stars are generally more luminous (the mass-luminosity relation); most stars have less mass than the Sun, the smallest true stars are about 1/12 of a solar mass, and stars near 100 solar masses are extremely rare.

On the H-R diagram, luminosity is plotted on the vertical axis and temperature or spectral class on the horizontal axis; about 90 percent of stars are main-sequence stars, giants occupy the upper right (cool but luminous, hence enormous), and white dwarfs occupy the lower left (hot but dim, hence tiny).

Spectral classes O, B, A, F, G, K, and M order stars from hottest to coolest (with L, T, and Y added for cooler objects); Annie Cannon created the mnemonic 'Oh Be A Fine Girl, Kiss Me' to remember the order.

About half of all stars are binary stars - two stars that orbit each other, bound together by gravity; measuring their orbits and applying Newton's version of Kepler's third law allows astronomers to calculate stellar masses.

The magnitude system ranks brightness backwards - brighter objects have smaller or more negative magnitudes (Sirius is -1.5, Venus -4.4 at brightest, the Sun -26.8); absolute magnitude compares stars as if they sat at a standard reference distance.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Temperatures quoted for individual star colors vary slightly across sources and editions (e.g., the Sun is quoted as about 5,500 C by NASA and about 6,000 K by OpenStax).
positions: OpenStax Astronomy 2e Table 17.1: Sun is yellow at about 6,000 K; examples run from blue 25,000 K to red 3,000 K.
NASA's Sun pages quote the photosphere at about 5,500 C, which equals about 5,800 K.
The previous verified research for this topic (2026-08-21) recorded the same OpenStax table values.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses OpenStax Table 17.1 values for star color-temperature examples and cites OpenStax, while keeping the wording 'about' for all figures; the Sun is described as a yellow G star at about 6,000 K in the color-temperature context.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The fraction of stars that are binaries is quoted differently by different sources.
positions: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 18.2: 'About half the stars are binary stars.'
Some surveys and secondary sources quote higher or lower fractions depending on how binaries are detected and counted.
The previous verified research for this topic (2026-08-21) recorded the OpenStax statement.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states that roughly half of all stars are binaries and cites OpenStax 18.2; no other figure is asserted.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The exact boundary temperature of O stars varies by source (OpenStax says hottest O stars exceed about 28,000 K).
positions: OpenStax Astronomy 2e 17.3: 'in the hottest O stars (those with temperatures over 28,000 K)'.
Other references occasionally quote 30,000 K or higher for the O class boundary.
The previous verified research for this topic (2026-08-21) recorded the OpenStax figure.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson avoids asserting a precise O-class temperature and only states that O is the hottest class in the OBAFGKM ordering, citing OpenStax 17.3.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced all generic draft boilerplate with source-verified content on what a star is, stellar properties, the H-R diagram, spectral classes, magnitudes, and binary stars.

Checked every quantitative figure against NASA and OpenStax: color-temperature table values (25,000 K to 3,000 K; Sun about 6,000 K), about 90 percent main-sequence stars, about half binary stars, smallest true stars about 1/12 solar mass, stars near 100 solar masses rare.

Used the simplified 'standard reference distance' wording for absolute magnitude because the live OpenStax 17.1 page truncated before its absolute-magnitude subsection and no Tier A/B source checked in this pass stated the 10-parsec convention.

Used for original synthesis only.
